reason: Tried to break it and could not. Downloaded the archive.org OCR of Porter’s 1914 Humphrey Milford volume (miscellanyofjapa00yosh) and read section 92 in place under its heading On the Waste of Time: “But his instructor said, ‘A beginner ought never to have a second arrow ; for as long as he relies upon the other, he will be careless with his first one. At each shot he ought to think that he is bound to settle it with this particular shaft at any cost.’” Both sentences are Porter’s word for word, consecutive and complete inside the instructor’s quotation marks; the only difference is the period spacing before the semicolon. No drift toward Keene or Sansom, whose wording differs. Both sentences fall between the running heads for pp. 74 and 75, so p. 74 is right, though the source cites only the section, and Porter’s section 92 is the standard section 92. The speaker is the instructor and is named in parentheses after the locator, as rule 5 asks. shipped.js: not shipped, nothing near, Kenkō 0 of 3, not banned. In scope (fourteenth-century zuihitsu, 1914 translation), publishable, on theme, one of the best known passages of the work. Essay is the form. Source leads with the name, no dash, 119 characters. One nicety, not a refutation: Essays in Idleness is the title of Sansom’s (1911) and Keene’s (1967) translations, not Porter’s, whose book is The Miscellany of a Japanese Priest; a reader hunting a Porter Essays in Idleness will not find one. The verifier weighed this and kept the usual English title, which is defensible since translator and year fix the wording; the alternative in betterCitation uses Porter’s own title and fits at 136 characters.
